Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Ravi is a 36-year-old South Asian man who has been an accountant for over a decade. His occupation demands meticulous attention to detail and a calm demeanor, yet his recent experience at work suggests otherwise. Ravi recently became superalert in the office, constantly scanning his surroundings, on guard against potential threats that he feels might emerge from any corner. Ravi’s traumatic event occurred during his childhood when he witnessed domestic violence between his parents. The vivid memories of those moments still haunt him. One particularly searing memory involves a night when his father physically lashed out at his mother in front of Ravi and his siblings. The sounds, the shouting, the physicality of that moment remain etched in his mind. Even now, the mere sight of someone raising their hand can trigger a flood of terror and a re-experience of that night’s horror. These memories are not just fleeting thoughts; they are visceral experiences that leave Ravi feeling physically reactive. For instance, at work, a sudden loud noise or an unexpected phone call can cause his heart to race and his body to tense up as if he were back in that traumatic moment. The constant state of alertness has made it difficult for him to focus on his tasks, leading to several errors and a noticeable decline in his performance. Ravi’s struggle to verbalize these memories further complicates matters. He can vividly recall the sights and sounds but struggles to articulate them into coherent sentences. This nonverbal memory often surfaces unexpectedly, triggered by mundane elements like the sound of breaking glass or a sudden shadow that resembles his father's figure from those nights. This fragmented and unprocessed trauma has led Ravi to develop avoidance behaviors that have had significant consequences in both his personal and professional life. His heightened hypervigilance and fear of potential threats made him reluctant to socialize or even leave the house at times, leading to further isolation. At work, he began avoiding interactions with colleagues and clients, which affected his job performance and strained relationships with coworkers. His recent divorce is a direct consequence of these avoidance behaviors. His wife found it increasingly difficult to connect with him, as Ravi had become distant and emotionally unavailable due to the constant fear and hypervigilance. He would often withdraw during conversations or tense up at unexpected sounds, making it challenging for her to feel secure in their relationship. Ravi’s negative appraisals further exacerbate his symptoms. He feels that the people responsible for those traumatic events—his father primarily—have faced no consequences for their actions, which leaves Ravi feeling a deep sense of injustice and helplessness. This belief has led him to conclude that he cannot prevent bad things from happening again, which only intensifies his hypervigilance. The constant state of misery and the inability to find happiness have become overwhelming for Ravi. He had come to believe that he would never be able to reclaim his former self or feel safe in his surroundings. It was a particularly intense episode at work—a sudden noise that triggered a flashback—that finally pushed him to seek help. The fear of losing his job and the realization that his quality of life was deteriorating made him recognize that he needed professional support. Ravi is now at a crossroads, feeling both afraid and hopeful. His primary fear is that he will never escape the grip of these traumatic memories and that they will continue to control his life. At the same time, he hopes for a way to process his experiences, regain some sense of safety and happiness, and reclaim his professional and personal life from the shadows cast by those painful memories.
